title: Empirical Asset Pricing with Polars
text:
About
A worked book for empirical asset pricing using Python Polars and local WRDS Parquet files. The chapters build from size portfolios to factor adjustment, double sorts, and Fama–MacBeth regression, inspired by Bali, Engle, and Murray’s Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns. AnomalyLab is an independent numerical reference, not a reader dependency.
The methods examples compare implementations on the same inputs. The final chapter compares reconstructed size summaries with the published Table 9.1. The book does not redistribute WRDS data.
See the Data chapter for the inputs. The WRDS table list includes their source update dates.

title: 1  Data
text:
1.1 WRDS tables
The examples read local Parquet files through era_pl.load_parquet(). The DATA_DIR setting points to the data root, and each table lives at DATA_DIR/schema/table.parquet. See the repository’s setup instructions to render the book with your own copies. The repository does not include the licensed WRDS data.
The table lists the inputs used in this build. The source update date comes from the metadata embedded in each Parquet file, read with db2pq. It is not the sample end date or the date the file was downloaded.

Most examples use CRSP’s newer CIZ files. The Table 9.1 replication instead uses legacy CRSP (SIZ), the format available when Bali, Engle, and Murray wrote the book. The local legacy exports are newer than their original snapshot. CIZ is not a drop-in substitute for legacy monthly returns: the two formats differ, for example, in the timing of dividend reinvestment. See CRSP’s comparison of the formats.

title: 1  Data
text:
1.2 Other input
The Table 9.1 replication also uses the BLS all-items CPI for urban consumers, not seasonally adjusted, from FRED, to express market capitalizations in December 2012 dollars. This file does not come from WRDS.

title: 2  Size portfolios
text:
2.1 Read the stock-month panel
This pilot forms monthly size quintiles and measures their next-month returns. It uses CRSP CIZ, a short historical subset (2000–2002 holding months), and breakpoints computed from all eligible observations rather than NYSE-only breakpoints. Its purpose is to compare the Polars sort with AnomalyLab on identical inputs, not to match the textbook’s tables.
Use ordinary U.S.-incorporated common shares of corporations on the NYSE, AMEX, and Nasdaq at formation. Use positive market capitalization for both the sort and the portfolio weights. Don’t require a stock to meet the same screen in the holding month: keep its reported CIZ return if present, including a return for a delisting month when available.
import polars as pl
from era_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(2000, 1, 1)
last = pl.date(2002, 12, 1)
monthly = (
    load_parquet("msf_v2", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("mthcaldt").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-1mo"), last))
)
stock_months = monthly.select("permno", "month")
assert stock_months.collect().is_duplicated().sum() == 0, "Duplicate stock-months"

formation = (
    monthly.filter(
        pl.col("securitytype") == "EQTY",
        pl.col("securitysubtype") == "COM",
        pl.col("sharetype") == "NS",
        pl.col("usincflg") == "Y",
        pl.col("issuertype").is_in(["ACOR", "CORP"]),
        pl.col("primaryexch").is_in(["A", "N", "Q"]),
        pl.col("tradingstatusflg") == "A",
        pl.col("conditionaltype") == "RW",
        pl.col("mthcap") > 0,
    )
    .select(
        "permno",
        pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo").alias("month"),
        pl.col("mthcap").alias("size"),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
)
returns = monthly.select("permno", "month", pl.col("mthret").alias("ret"))
panel = formation.join(returns, on=["permno", "month"], how="left").collect()
complete = panel.filter(pl.col("ret").is_finite())
print(f"{panel.height:,} formation observations; {complete.height:,} with a usable return.")

218,291 formation observations; 215,991 with a usable return.
The join advances the calendar by exactly one month. It does not jump a gap to the next available observed return. For this parity check, we follow AnomalyLab by dropping missing holding-period returns before computing breakpoints. That can change the portfolios using information that wasn’t known at formation. A backtest should instead freeze the breakpoints and assignments at formation, then handle missing returns separately.

title: 2  Size portfolios
text:
2.2 Sort within each month
Use linear quantiles and right-closed bins, like the reference’s pandas.qcut quintiles. Values equal to a breakpoint stay in the lower bin. Stop rather than silently breaking ties if quantile edges coincide.

probs = [0, .2, .4, .6, .8, 1]
edges = [f"q{i}" for i in range(len(probs))]
cutoffs = complete.group_by("month").agg(
    pl.col("size").quantile(q, interpolation="linear").alias(edge)
    for q, edge in zip(probs, edges)
)
assert cutoffs.height > 0, "No complete stock-months"
assert not cutoffs.select(
    pl.any_horizontal(pl.col(a) >= pl.col(b) for a, b in zip(edges, edges[1:])).any()
).item(), "Non-unique quantile edges"

members = (
    complete.join(cutoffs, on="month")
    .with_columns(
        quintile=1 + pl.sum_horizontal(
            (pl.col("size") > pl.col(edge)).cast(pl.Int32) for edge in edges[1:-1]
        )
    )
    .select("permno", "month", "size", "ret", "quintile")
)

title: 2  Size portfolios
text:
2.3 Compare returns
Compute one equal-weighted and one value-weighted return per month and quintile. Then take the arithmetic mean over months. The spread is large minus small. Returns in the table are percentages per month; the calculations use decimals.

monthly_returns = members.group_by("month", "quintile").agg(
    equal_weighted=pl.col("ret").mean(),
    value_weighted=(pl.col("ret") * pl.col("size")).sum() / pl.col("size").sum(),
).sort("month", "quintile")
assert monthly_returns.group_by("month").len()["len"].eq(5).all()

small = monthly_returns.filter(pl.col("quintile") == 1)
large = monthly_returns.filter(pl.col("quintile") == 5)
spread = large.join(small, on="month", suffix="_small").select(
    "month",
    pl.lit(6, dtype=pl.Int32).alias("quintile"),
    (pl.col("equal_weighted") - pl.col("equal_weighted_small")).alias("equal_weighted"),
    (pl.col("value_weighted") - pl.col("value_weighted_small")).alias("value_weighted"),
)
all_returns = pl.concat([monthly_returns, spread])
summary = all_returns.group_by("quintile").agg(
    pl.len().alias("months"),
    (100 * pl.col("equal_weighted").mean()).round(3).alias("equal_weighted_pct"),
    (100 * pl.col("value_weighted").mean()).round(3).alias("value_weighted_pct"),
).sort("quintile").with_columns(
    portfolio=pl.when(pl.col("quintile") == 6).then(pl.lit("Large − small"))
    .otherwise(pl.col("quintile").cast(pl.String))
).drop("quintile").select("portfolio", "months", "equal_weighted_pct", "value_weighted_pct")

title: 2  Size portfolios
text:
2.4 Risk-adjusted returns
A portfolio’s average return includes compensation for exposures to common risk factors. We estimate Fama–French three-factor alphas by regressing each portfolio’s excess return on the market excess return, SMB, and HML. Subtract the risk-free rate from each quintile’s return. For the long–short spread the two risk-free rates cancel.

factors = (
    load_parquet("factors_monthly", "ff")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start())
    .select("month", "mktrf", "smb", "hml", "rf")
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    .collect()
)
factor_data = (
    all_returns
    .join(factors, on="month", validate="m:1")
    .unpivot(
        on=["equal_weighted", "value_weighted"],
        index=["month", "quintile", "mktrf", "smb", "hml", "rf"],
        variable_name="weighting",
        value_name="ret",
    )
    .with_columns(
        excess=pl.when(pl.col("quintile") == 6)
        .then(pl.col("ret"))
        .otherwise(pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"))
    )
    .sort("month")
)

The intercept is monthly alpha. We use Bartlett Newey–West standard errors with three lags and no small-sample correction, matching the numeric AnomalyLab calculation. The regressions use only 36 months, so these are illustrations of the method rather than a test of the size premium.

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

assert factor_data.height == 2 * all_returns.height
assert not any(factor_data.select("mktrf", "smb", "hml", "rf").null_count().row(0))

fits = {
    key: smf.ols("excess ~ mktrf + smb + hml", data=series.to_pandas()).fit(
        cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 3, "use_correction": False}
    )
    for key, series in factor_data.group_by("quintile", "weighting")
}
alphas = pl.DataFrame([
    {"quintile": quintile, "weighting": weighting, "months": int(fm.nobs),
     "alpha_pct": 100 * fm.params["Intercept"], "t": fm.tvalues["Intercept"]}
    for (quintile, weighting), fm in fits.items()
]).sort("quintile", "weighting")
alphas.with_columns(
    portfolio=pl.when(pl.col("quintile") == 6).then(pl.lit("Large − small"))
    .otherwise(pl.col("quintile").cast(pl.String)),
    alpha_pct=pl.col("alpha_pct").round(3), t=pl.col("t").round(3),
).select("portfolio", "weighting", "months", "alpha_pct", "t")

title: 3  Size and momentum
text:
3.1 Measure momentum
A stock’s past returns may help explain its future returns. But the apparent momentum effect could differ with size. Here we compare two ways to sort on both characteristics.
For a portfolio held in month \(t\), we measure size at the end of month \(t-1\) and compound returns from months \(t-12\) through \(t-2\) to measure momentum. Skipping month \(t-1\) separates the momentum signal from the most recent return. The holding-period outcome is the return in month \(t\).
Work with the same holding months as in Chapter 2. For holding month \(t\), market equity is observed at the end of \(t-1\). Momentum compounds returns from \(t-12\) through \(t-2\), skipping \(t-1\). The calendar window must have all 11 monthly returns, so it cannot jump over a missing month.
import polars as pl
from era_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(2000, 1, 1)
last = pl.date(2002, 12, 1)

msf = (
    load_parquet("msf_v2", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("mthcaldt").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-12mo"), last))
)
rets = (
    msf
    .select("permno", "month", ret="mthret")
    .collect()
    .sort("permno", "month")
)
assert not rets.select("permno", "month").is_duplicated().any()

momentum = (
    rets
    .rolling("month", period="11mo", group_by="permno", closed="left")
    .agg(
        momentum=(1 + pl.col("ret")).product() - 1,
        n_months=pl.col("ret").count(),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("n_months") == 11)
    .select("permno", "month", "momentum")
)

size = (
    msf
    .filter(
        pl.col("securitytype") == "EQTY",
        pl.col("securitysubtype") == "COM",
        pl.col("sharetype") == "NS",
        pl.col("usincflg") == "Y",
        pl.col("issuertype").is_in(["ACOR", "CORP"]),
        pl.col("primaryexch").is_in(["A", "N", "Q"]),
        pl.col("tradingstatusflg") == "A",
        pl.col("conditionaltype") == "RW",
        pl.col("mthcap") > 0,
    )
    .select("permno", "month", size="mthcap")
    .collect()
)
characteristics = (
    size
    .join(momentum, on=["permno", "month"], validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    .join(rets, on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1")
)

title: 3  Size and momentum
text:
3.2 Summarize the characteristics
We first restrict attention to observations for which both characteristics are available. These descriptive calculations do not use the holding-month return.

signals = (
    characteristics
    .filter(pl.col("size").is_finite() & pl.col("momentum").is_finite())
    .with_columns(log_size=pl.col("size").log())
)

monthly_summary = (
    signals
    .group_by("month")
    .agg(
        stocks=pl.len(),
        median_momentum=pl.col("momentum").median(),
        corr_size_momentum=pl.corr("log_size", "momentum"),
    )
)

monthly_summary.select(
    avg_stocks=pl.col("stocks").mean().round(0),
    avg_median_momentum_pct=(100 * pl.col("median_momentum").mean()).round(2),
    avg_corr=pl.col("corr_size_momentum").mean().round(3),
)

The correlation is cross-sectional in each month; we give each month equal weight. Persistence asks a different question: how closely does a stock’s momentum today resemble its own momentum at an earlier date? Match the dates rather than shifting by a number of rows, so a stock missing a month does not silently appear to have been observed in it.

def momentum_persistence(months):
    past = signals.select(
        "permno",
        pl.col("month").dt.offset_by(f"{months}mo"),
        pl.col("momentum").alias("momentum_past"),
    )

    return (
        signals
        .join(past, on=["permno", "month"], validate="1:1")
        .group_by("month")
        .agg(correlation=pl.corr("momentum", "momentum_past"))
        .select(lag_months=pl.lit(months),
                months=pl.col("correlation").is_finite().sum(),
                average_corr=pl.col("correlation").filter(
                    pl.col("correlation").is_finite()
                ).mean().round(3))
    )

pl.concat([momentum_persistence(h) for h in [1, 3, 12]])

title: 3  Size and momentum
text:
3.3 Sort the stocks into portfolios
An independent sort finds size and momentum breakpoints separately in each month. A dependent sort finds momentum breakpoints within each size group. The second approach ranks firms against other firms of similar size.
As in AnomalyLab’s three-group implementation, we use 30th and 70th percentile cutoffs, with observations exactly on a cutoff assigned to the lower group. For this comparison we drop observations with missing holding-month returns before forming groups, as AnomalyLab does. In an investable backtest, form the groups before checking which returns are available, then handle missing returns separately.

def sort_into_three(data, characteristic, by, group):
    x = pl.col(characteristic)
    low = x.quantile(0.30, interpolation="linear").over(by)
    high = x.quantile(0.70, interpolation="linear").over(by)

    return data.with_columns(
        pl.when(x <= low).then(1).when(x <= high).then(2).otherwise(3)
        .alias(group)
    )

sort_sample = signals.filter(pl.col("ret").is_finite())
size_groups = sort_into_three(sort_sample, "size", "month", "size_group")

independent = sort_into_three(size_groups, "momentum", "month", "momentum_group")
dependent = sort_into_three(
    size_groups, "momentum", ["month", "size_group"], "momentum_group"
)

title: 3  Size and momentum
text:
3.4 Compare the portfolio returns
For each sort, first compute the nine monthly returns. Then subtract the low-momentum return from the high-momentum return within each size group. The table averages those monthly spreads and reports percentage points per month. Value weights are the market capitalizations used at formation.

def portfolio_returns(groups):
    return (
        groups
        .group_by("month", "size_group", "momentum_group")
        .agg(
            equal_weighted=pl.col("ret").mean(),
            value_weighted=(pl.col("ret") * pl.col("size")).sum() / pl.col("size").sum(),
        )
    )

def momentum_spread(returns, design):
    keys = ["month", "size_group"]
    low = returns.filter(pl.col("momentum_group") == 1)
    high = returns.filter(pl.col("momentum_group") == 3)

    return (
        high
        .join(low, on=keys, suffix="_low", validate="1:1")
        .group_by("size_group")
        .agg(
            months=pl.len(),
            equal_weighted_pct=(
                100 * (pl.col("equal_weighted") - pl.col("equal_weighted_low")).mean()
            ).round(3),
            value_weighted_pct=(
                100 * (pl.col("value_weighted") - pl.col("value_weighted_low")).mean()
            ).round(3),
        )
        .with_columns(sort=pl.lit(design))
    )

independent_returns = portfolio_returns(independent)
dependent_returns = portfolio_returns(dependent)

(
    pl.concat([momentum_spread(independent_returns, "Independent"),
               momentum_spread(dependent_returns, "Dependent")])
    .select("sort", "size_group", "months", "equal_weighted_pct", "value_weighted_pct")
    .sort("sort", "size_group")
)

The two designs need not produce the same portfolios or spreads. The independent design holds the absolute momentum thresholds fixed across size groups; the dependent design fills each size group with roughly the same proportions of low-, medium-, and high-momentum stocks.

title: 3  Size and momentum
text:
3.5 Track changes in momentum groups
The persistence correlations summarize how closely the levels of momentum move together. A transition matrix asks instead how often a stock remains in the same group. Assign each stock to a momentum group every month using the same 30th and 70th percentile cutoffs, without conditioning on the holding-month return.
Match the same stock exactly 12 calendar months later. The percentages are conditional on having a momentum group in both months. We pool stock-month pairs before calculating each row’s shares, rather than averaging monthly shares. A month with more matched stocks therefore gets more weight.

momentum_groups = (
    sort_into_three(signals, "momentum", "month", "momentum_group")
    .select("permno", "month", "momentum_group")
)
at_start = momentum_groups.select(
    "permno", "month", start_group="momentum_group"
)
one_year_later = momentum_groups.select(
    "permno",
    pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("-12mo"),
    end_group="momentum_group",
)
transition_pairs = at_start.join(
    one_year_later, on=["permno", "month"], validate="1:1"
)

transition_matrix = (
    transition_pairs
    .group_by("start_group")
    .agg(
        pairs=pl.len(),
        low_pct=100 * (pl.col("end_group") == 1).mean(),
        middle_pct=100 * (pl.col("end_group") == 2).mean(),
        high_pct=100 * (pl.col("end_group") == 3).mean(),
    )
    .sort("start_group")
)
transition_matrix.with_columns(pl.col("low_pct", "middle_pct", "high_pct").round(1))

Each row shows where stocks starting in that group end up after a year. The diagonal gives the percentage that remains in the same group. This is not a measure of how many stocks drop out of the sample.
AnomalyLab also pools counts before dividing by the row totals, but it pairs dates by position in the sequence of distinct observed months. That agrees with a 12-month calendar match here because the sequence has no missing months. In a panel with a missing month across all stocks, the calendar join still matches observations exactly one year apart.

title: 4  Fama–MacBeth regressions
text:
4.1 Prepare the monthly panel
A portfolio sort compares returns across groups. A Fama–MacBeth regression instead estimates how returns vary with several characteristics at once. We estimate one cross-sectional regression per holding month, then give each month equal weight when averaging its coefficients.
We use market equity measured at formation and momentum from months \(t-12\) through \(t-2\) to explain the return in holding month \(t\).
Work with the same holding months as in Chapter 2. For holding month \(t\), market equity is observed at the end of \(t-1\). Momentum compounds returns from \(t-12\) through \(t-2\), skipping \(t-1\). The calendar window must have all 11 monthly returns, so it cannot jump over a missing month.
import polars as pl
from era_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(2000, 1, 1)
last = pl.date(2002, 12, 1)

msf = (
    load_parquet("msf_v2", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("mthcaldt").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-12mo"), last))
)
rets = (
    msf
    .select("permno", "month", ret="mthret")
    .collect()
    .sort("permno", "month")
)
assert not rets.select("permno", "month").is_duplicated().any()

momentum = (
    rets
    .rolling("month", period="11mo", group_by="permno", closed="left")
    .agg(
        momentum=(1 + pl.col("ret")).product() - 1,
        n_months=pl.col("ret").count(),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("n_months") == 11)
    .select("permno", "month", "momentum")
)

size = (
    msf
    .filter(
        pl.col("securitytype") == "EQTY",
        pl.col("securitysubtype") == "COM",
        pl.col("sharetype") == "NS",
        pl.col("usincflg") == "Y",
        pl.col("issuertype").is_in(["ACOR", "CORP"]),
        pl.col("primaryexch").is_in(["A", "N", "Q"]),
        pl.col("tradingstatusflg") == "A",
        pl.col("conditionaltype") == "RW",
        pl.col("mthcap") > 0,
    )
    .select("permno", "month", size="mthcap")
    .collect()
)
characteristics = (
    size
    .join(momentum, on=["permno", "month"], validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo"))
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first, last))
    .join(rets, on=["permno", "month"], how="left", validate="1:1")
)
import statspai as sp

fm_data = (
    characteristics
    .with_columns(log_size=pl.col("size").log())
    .select("permno", "month", "ret", "log_size", "momentum")
    .filter(pl.all_horizontal(pl.col("ret", "log_size", "momentum").is_finite()))
    .sort("month", "permno")
)
We take the natural log of market equity. Returns and momentum are expressed as decimals, and the regressors are not standardized within month.

title: 4  Fama–MacBeth regressions
text:
4.2 Estimate the two-step regression
Set time="month" to identify the cross-sections. lags=3 applies a Newey–West adjustment to the monthly coefficient series, not to each cross-sectional regression. The estimates are the same in both columns; the standard errors need not be.

fm = sp.fama_macbeth("ret ~ log_size + momentum", data=fm_data, time="month")
fm_nw = sp.fama_macbeth(
    "ret ~ log_size + momentum", data=fm_data, time="month", lags=3
)


sp.regtable(
    fm, fm_nw,
    model_labels=["FM-t", "FM-NW (3 lags)"],
    keep=["Intercept", "log_size", "momentum"],
    fmt=4,
    stats=["N"],
    diagnostics=False,
)

AnomalyLab uses the same monthly regressions on these inputs, but its Newey–West covariance does not apply StatsPAI’s finite-sample correction. For \(T\) months, StatsPAI multiplies that covariance by \(T/(T-1)\), and uses a Student \(t\) reference with \(T-1\) degrees of freedom rather than a normal reference. For validation, we check the individual monthly coefficients first, then compare standard errors after aligning the finite-sample correction.

title: 5  Size and illiquidity
text:
5.1 From daily data to monthly illiquidity
We can sort on two characteristics to see, for example, whether the spread between illiquid and liquid stocks differs across size portfolios. We use monthly market capitalization and a measure constructed from daily prices and volume. As in the size chapter, the holding months are January 2000 through December 2002; this is a methods comparison, not a replication of published estimates.
Following Amihud (2002), divide each absolute daily return by daily dollar volume, then average the ratios. Here we average within each stock-month, require 10 usable days, and scale by one million for readability. CRSP’s dlyprcvol approximates dollar volume as price times shares traded. We exclude zero volume and use only information through the formation month.
import polars as pl
from era_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(2000, 1, 1)
last = pl.date(2002, 12, 1)

illiq = (
    load_parquet("dsf_v2", "crsp")
    .filter(
        pl.col("dlycaldt").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-1mo"), last, closed="left"),
        pl.col("dlydelflg") == "N",
        pl.col("dlyret").is_finite(),
        pl.col("dlyprcvol").is_finite(),
        pl.col("dlyprcvol") > 0,
    )
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.col("dlycaldt").dt.month_start(),
        daily_illiq=1e6 * pl.col("dlyret").abs() / pl.col("dlyprcvol"),
    )
    .group_by("permno", "month")
    .agg(illiq=pl.col("daily_illiq").mean(), days=pl.len())
    .filter(pl.col("days") >= 10)
    .select("permno", "month", "illiq")
)

title: 5  Size and illiquidity
text:
5.2 Align formation and holding months
We apply the same formation screen as in the size chapter. Both characteristics are measured in month \(t\); the return is for month \(t+1\). For the AnomalyLab comparison we keep only rows with a usable holding return before sorting. As in the size chapter, this complete-case convention is not a recommended way to form portfolios in a real-time backtest.

monthly = (
    load_parquet("msf_v2", "crsp")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("mthcaldt").dt.month_start())
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(first.dt.offset_by("-1mo"), last))
)

formation = (
    monthly
    .filter(
        pl.col("securitytype") == "EQTY",
        pl.col("securitysubtype") == "COM",
        pl.col("sharetype") == "NS",
        pl.col("usincflg") == "Y",
        pl.col("issuertype").is_in(["ACOR", "CORP"]),
        pl.col("primaryexch").is_in(["A", "N", "Q"]),
        pl.col("tradingstatusflg") == "A",
        pl.col("conditionaltype") == "RW",
        pl.col("mthcap") > 0,
    )
    .select("permno", "month", size="mthcap")
    .join(illiq, on=["permno", "month"], validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(month=pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("1mo"))
)

returns = monthly.select("permno", "month", ret="mthret")
stocks = (
    formation
    .join(returns, on=["permno", "month"], validate="1:1")
    .filter(pl.col("ret").is_finite())
    .collect()
)

title: 5  Size and illiquidity
section: 5.3 Sort independently and within size groups

title: 5  Size and illiquidity
text:
5.4 Compare monthly returns
For each size group, take the monthly return on its most illiquid quintile minus that on its most liquid quintile. The table reports average spreads in percentage points per month.

def portfolio_returns(grouped):
    return (
        grouped
        .group_by("month", "size_group", "illiq_group")
        .agg(
            equal_weighted=pl.col("ret").mean(),
            value_weighted=(pl.col("ret") * pl.col("size")).sum() / pl.col("size").sum(),
        )
    )

def spread(returns):
    keys = ["month", "size_group"]
    low = returns.filter(pl.col("illiq_group") == 1).select(*keys, "equal_weighted", "value_weighted")
    high = returns.filter(pl.col("illiq_group") == 5).select(*keys, "equal_weighted", "value_weighted")
    return high.join(low, on=keys, suffix="_low", validate="1:1").select(
        *keys,
        equal_weighted=pl.col("equal_weighted") - pl.col("equal_weighted_low"),
        value_weighted=pl.col("value_weighted") - pl.col("value_weighted_low"),
    )

sorts = {"Independent": independent, "Dependent": dependent}
portfolios = {name: portfolio_returns(grouped) for name, grouped in sorts.items()}
spreads = pl.concat(
    spread(ret).with_columns(sort=pl.lit(name)) for name, ret in portfolios.items()
)

(
    spreads.group_by("sort", "size_group")
    .agg(
        months=pl.len(),
        equal_weighted_pct=(100 * pl.col("equal_weighted").mean()).round(3),
        value_weighted_pct=(100 * pl.col("value_weighted").mean()).round(3),
    )
    .sort("sort", "size_group")
)

title: 6  Replicating the size summary
text:
6.1 Reconstruct the published sample
The earlier chapters compare two implementations on a common input. Here the benchmark is an actual published result: Table 9.1 in Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016), Empirical Asset Pricing, §9.2. They calculate statistics across stocks each month, then average those statistics over the 594 months from June 1963 through November 2012.
The book was published in 2016, well before CRSP’s CIZ format. This replication uses the legacy (SIZ) monthly stock and names files, not the CIZ files used in the earlier chapters. Our legacy snapshot is newer than the authors’ original data, even though we use the same sample dates. See the WRDS table list for the embedded update dates.
Use the share code in force at the end of each month. Keep share codes 10 and 11, without adding an exchange screen. The book’s measure uses the absolute alternate price and shares outstanding. CRSP records shares in thousands; dividing their product by 1,000 gives market capitalization in millions of dollars. Treat zeros as missing.
import polars as pl
from era_pl import load_parquet

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)

prices = (
    load_parquet("msf", "crsp")
    .filter(pl.col("date").is_between(first, last.dt.month_end()))
    .with_columns(
        month=pl.col("date").dt.month_start(),
        cap=pl.when((pl.col("altprc") != 0) & (pl.col("shrout") > 0))
        .then((pl.col("altprc") * pl.col("shrout")).abs() / 1000),
    )
    .select("permno", "month", "cap")
)
names = (
    load_parquet("msenames", "crsp")
    .select("permno", "namedt", "nameendt", "shrcd")
    .sort("namedt")
)
sample = (
    prices
    .with_columns(month_end=pl.col("month").dt.month_end())
    .sort("month_end")
    .join_asof(
        names, left_on="month_end", right_on="namedt",
        by="permno", check_sortedness=False,
    )
    .filter(pl.col("month_end") <= pl.col("nameendt"), pl.col("shrcd").is_in([10, 11]))
    .select("permno", "month", "cap")
)
For the annual measure, join each stock to its capitalization at the most recent June. A stock without a record for that particular June has no annual value. We do not carry forward an older June observation.
june_caps = (
    prices
    .filter(pl.col("month").dt.month() == 6)
    .select("permno", june="month", cap_june="cap")
)
june_year = pl.col("month").dt.year() - (pl.col("month").dt.month() < 6)
sample = (
    sample
    .with_columns(june=pl.date(june_year, 6, 1))
    .join(june_caps, on=["permno", "june"], how="left", validate="m:1")
)

title: 6  Replicating the size summary
section: 6.2 Compare four measures of size and their logs
text:
6.2 Compare four measures of size and their logs
Convert nominal market capitalization to December 2012 dollars using the BLS CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted. Use the CPI for the current observation month for both the monthly and the June-based measures, as in the book.

cpi = pl.read_csv("data/cpi-aucns.csv", try_parse_dates=True).rename(
    {"observation_date": "month", "CPIAUCNS": "cpi"}
)
cpi_2012 = cpi.filter(pl.col("month") == pl.date(2012, 12, 1))["cpi"].item()

sizes = (
    sample
    .join(cpi.lazy(), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(
        cap_real=pl.col("cap") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
        cap_june_real=pl.col("cap_june") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
    )
    .collect()
)
assert sizes["month"].n_unique() == 594
assert sizes["cpi"].null_count() == 0
sizes = sizes.with_columns(
    pl.col(var).log().alias(f"log_{var}")
    for var in ["cap", "cap_real", "cap_june", "cap_june_real"]
)

The mean of the monthly medians describes the middle stock in a typical month. It is not a median calculated once on the pooled stock-month data.

def cross_section(data, variable):
    x = pl.col(variable)
    return (
        data
        .group_by("month")
        .agg(
            mean=x.mean(), sd=x.std(), skew=x.skew(bias=False),
            kurtosis=x.kurtosis(fisher=True, bias=False),
            minimum=x.min(),
            p05=x.quantile(.05, interpolation="linear"),
            p25=x.quantile(.25, interpolation="linear"),
            median=x.median(),
            p75=x.quantile(.75, interpolation="linear"),
            p95=x.quantile(.95, interpolation="linear"),
            maximum=x.max(), n=x.count(),
        )
        .select(pl.lit(variable).alias("measure"), pl.exclude("month").mean())
    )

stats = pl.concat([
    cross_section(sizes, var)
    for var in ["cap", "log_cap", "cap_real", "log_cap_real",
                "cap_june", "log_cap_june", "cap_june_real", "log_cap_june_real"]
])
